history: The system's pulsar was detected in 2234; the ancient circumbinary planet Methuselah was discovered in 2267, revolutionizing understanding of planetary formation.
Chronos Observatory was established in 2489 to study relativistic effects near the binary pair, becoming the foremost pulsar research facility in known space.
The small colony on Testament was founded in 2534 by support staff who chose to remain permanently rather than rotate back to civilization.
description: Void Dancer's Binary preserves the corpses of two stars that died billions of years before Earth formed, their remains locked in an eternal gravitational embrace. The white dwarf Dancer slowly surrenders its mass to its Partner, a millisecond pulsar spinning 200 times per second, the transferred matter forming a visible stream of plasma that bridges the stellar remnants. Methuselah, the circumbinary planet, predates most stars in the galaxy—a witness to cosmic history that has outlived the suns that may have once warmed it.

The system exists for science. Chronos Observatory draws researchers from across known space to study pulsar physics, gravitational waves, and relativistic effects in one of the most extreme environments accessible to human technology. The time dilation near the pulsar is measurable: clocks there run slower than in normal space, a laboratory for testing theories that elsewhere remain purely mathematical. Access is restricted; only credentialed scientists and essential support personnel may enter the system.

Testament's 8,500 residents form an unusual community—support staff who chose exile in one of the galaxy's most hostile systems rather than return to civilization. They live deep underground, shielded from radiation that would kill in hours on the surface, sustained by fusion power and hydroponic farms. Asked why they stay, they speak of the view from Observatory windows: two stellar corpses dancing, a planet older than imagination, and the humbling reminder that humanity is young in a very old universe.
